consensus_summary: Righteousness primarily denotes a right legal and relational standing before God (justification)—often understood as a status imputed or granted by grace through faith—along with moral uprightness and conformity to God's standards.
book_summary: Righteousness is defined strictly as 'right-living'—specifically, the active living out of God's commandments. It rejects the paradigm that righteousness is primarily a legal standing with right-living merely as a subsequent fruit.
consensus_core_identification: A relational/forensic status of right standing before God, alongside moral conformity to His will.
book_core_identification: Active obedience and right-living; the execution of God's commandments.
boundary_disagreement: The book excludes 'right standing' or 'imputed legal status' from the definition of righteousness, restricting the term entirely to active moral conduct and obedience.
material_contradiction: The consensus maintains that in salvation contexts, righteousness is primarily a status conferred by God apart from works; the book asserts that righteousness is by definition the doing of works (living out God's commandments).
rationale: By defining righteousness exclusively as 'right-living' and 'commandments lived out,' the book explicitly rejects the primary consensus definition of righteousness as an imputed relational or legal standing before God, isolating and elevating what the consensus considers the secondary aspect (moral conduct) to be the sole meaning.
strongest_objection: Romans 4:4-8 (which the book cites) explicitly states that righteousness is imputed to the one 'that worketh not,' which prima facie contradicts the definition that righteousness is exclusively 'commandments lived out.'
